issues.legal_issue: When a landlord establishes a bona fide requirement for eviction, the court must assess comparative hardship by weighing the parties’ relative circumstances, and the tenant bears the burden of proving that eviction would cause greater hardship.
material_facts: The landlord’s need for the ground-floor premises for his sons’ electronic-goods business was found to be genuine because that business and the landlord’s cloth business were crowded into the landlord’s existing shop.
The tenant had run a cloth business in the premises for a long time, the shop was his only source of income, and the business had some goodwill.

The lower courts relied on the tenant’s business circumstances and the likely cost of obtaining other premises when finding that eviction from the ground floor would cause the tenant greater hardship.
issues.conclusion: The landlord bears the burden of establishing the eviction ground, but once that ground is established, the tenant bears the burden of proving greater hardship from eviction. The court must compare the parties’ relative hardship, considering all relevant circumstances; the fact of eviction alone does not establish hardship.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 13(1)(g) and 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947, Section 13(2) operates as a qualification to the eviction right under Section 13(1)(g). The landlord must prove the bona fide requirement, while the tenant must prove the greater hardship that would justify denying eviction. The court must assess the intensity of each side’s need and relevant circumstances, including available accommodation, business and family circumstances, likely future consequences, and the parties’ conduct. Mere displacement is not, by itself, hardship. The Court relied on Mst. Bega Begum v. Abdul Ahad Khan for the need to weigh the parties’ relative advantages and disadvantages and on Piper v. Harvery for the tenant’s burden to prove hardship beyond the ordinary consequence of eviction.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_case: The proceeding concerns a claim to evict a tenant under a rent-control regime.
predicates.landlord_need_established: The court has found that the landlord has a genuine and reasonable need for the premises.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding involves an established landlord need, the court compares the parties’ relative hardship and the tenant must prove that eviction would cause greater hardship.

issues.legal_issue: A court deciding comparative hardship in a rent-control eviction case must consider whether partial eviction would meet the landlord’s established need while avoiding unnecessary hardship to the tenant.
material_facts: The landlord’s bona fide need for the ground floor had been established, but the lower courts denied eviction from that part of the premises on comparative-hardship grounds.
The lower courts did not examine whether the tenant could be evicted from only part of the ground floor.
Evidence indicated that approximately 300 square feet were used for storage and waste material rather than the tenant’s business.
The Supreme Court considered the existing record insufficient to decide the comparative-hardship and partial-eviction questions itself.
issues.conclusion: The denial of eviction from the ground floor was set aside and the matter was remitted to the appellate court to determine comparative hardship and whether, and to what extent, partial eviction would meet the ends of justice.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates (Control) Act, 1947 expressly permits a decree for part of the premises where the court is satisfied that hardship would not be caused to either side by doing so. The court must consider whether partial eviction can satisfy the proved landlord requirement while preserving the tenant’s ability to continue business, and should frame issues and allow relevant evidence where needed.

rule.if: appeal_from_denial_of_eviction and landlord_need_established and lower_court_omitted_partial_eviction_review and unused_nonbusiness_area_exists

predicates.appeal_from_denial_of_eviction: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a refusal to order eviction from the premises at issue.
predicates.landlord_need_established: The court has found that the landlord has a genuine and reasonable need for the premises.
predicates.lower_court_omitted_partial_eviction_rev: The lower court decided comparative hardship without considering whether eviction from only part of the premises would suffice.
predicates.unused_nonbusiness_area_exists: Evidence shows that a portion of the premises is not being used for the tenant’s business.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges refusal of eviction despite an established landlord need, and the lower court omitted partial-eviction review despite evidence of an unused nonbusiness area, the refusal is set aside and the case is remitted for findings on comparative hardship and partial eviction.
